Thanks again for the demo today, Soojin — really helpful walkthrough. A few quick clarifying asks from our SRE/infra folks (I've copied ops-team):

1) Failover semantics: we need a one-paragraph description of how Redwood handles a single-region outage and an instance-level GPU OOM. Specifically: what switches (model variant fallback, cached KV re-use, cross-region warm standby) happen automatically, what requires operator config, and expected RTO for each path.

2) Rate limiting: are there per-token and per-request rate limits by default? Can we set a hard per-tenant TPS cap while allowing bursts? What happens to queued requests when capacity is exhausted?

3) Error budget accounting: how do we report and export error budgets? We care about 99.9% uptime windows vs token-level error rates (e.g., 5xx vs malformed prompts).

4) Comparison vs hyperscalers: our procurement team asked for a tight comparison vs the major cloud inference APIs (throughput, tail latency, fallthrough behavior when a zone degrades). If you could share a short matrix with measured numbers or guidance on where Redwood is intentionally different, that would be ideal.

Next steps on our side: ops will sketch benchmark scenarios and share a sample workload next week. Would love any recommended probes/tests you want us to include to exercise failover and rate-limiting behavior.

Thanks — HP

Hi Helen — great to chat, and appreciate the clear asks. High level answers below and I've attached a concise matrix and a short sample of demo logs to illustrate behaviors. Karthik and Marissa are looped in for technical detail and to propose test owners.

1) Failover semantics (short):
- Single-region outage: automatic routing to warm standby region if cross-region standby is enabled (configurable per-tenant). We keep KV cache validity windows; prefix caching reduces cold-starts on failover but some warm-up tokens expected. Typical RTO with warm standby: 30–120s depending on model size and KV warm-up.
- Instance-level GPU OOM: we preemptively fall back to either a compatible quantized variant (if model/catalog has one) or an autoscale replacement pod; small requests are transparently re-routed within 1–10s, larger batches may be retried.
- Operator controls: you can pin fallback policies, enable cross-region warm standby, or set aggressive cache retention.

2) Rate limiting:
- Default: per-API-key request QPS and per-token emission throttle.
- Tenant caps: you can set hard per-tenant TPS/Tokens-per-minute caps and define burst policies (steady-state vs burst windows). When capacity is exhausted we queue requests up to a configurable window (default 30s), then return 429 with a Retry-After and structured retry_hint explaining fallback options.

3) Error budget accounting:
- We expose time-windowed SLO dashboards (99.9/99.95) with breakdowns by 5xx vs latency breach vs token-truncation. Exports available via Prometheus/Graphite endpoints and CSV from the Console. Error budget policy is configurable per-route; alerts trigger when burn rate exceeds thresholds.

4) Hyperscaler comparison (summary):
- Throughput: Redwood focuses on sustained, predictable throughput on reserved pools; hyperscalers can scale elastically but often with more variance in tail latency under multi-tenant noisy neighbors.
- Tail latency: our runtime optimizations (KV prefix reuse and continuous batching) reduce token tail latency at steady-state relative to generic endpoint products.
- Fallthrough: Redwood offers more deterministic policy-driven fallbacks (model variant + region) with explicit warm-standby options; hyperscalers typically rely on global LB + autoscale which can lead to higher RTOs for large models.

Attached: redwood-vs-hyperscaler-failover-matrix-20270418.xlsx (simple matrix + recommended tests), demo-logs-sample-20270418.txt.

Suggested probes to include in your bench:
- Region failover: simulate region-level network blackhole and measure 90/95/99 pct RTO across model sizes.
- OOM recovery: send increasing batch sizes to force OOM and measure percent of requests auto-failed vs auto-fallbacked.
- Burst protection: send TPS bursts exceeding tenant cap and observe queueing behavior and 429 patterns.

I'll let Karthik/Marissa propose owners and timing. Happy to join a quick call to review the test plan.

Thanks for the clear ask, Soojin and Helen. I'll own the failover probes and provide a reproducible test harness. Quick notes / proposed test plan:

- Region failover probe:
  * Harness: k6 + a small proxy to flip egress route to simulate region blackout.
  * Metrics: RTO (time to first successful token), per-token tail latency (95/99/99.9), cold-start count, KV cache hit-rate.
  * Targets: small (L1) ~512-token model, medium (L2) ~2k tokens, large (L3) 8k tokens.

- OOM/instance-preempt probe:
  * Harness: ramped batch size until memory pressure triggers preemption. Capture how many requests get retried and fallback percent.
  * Metric: percent auto-fallback vs user-visible failures, time-to-success for retried requests.

- Rate-limit/burst probe:
  * Harness: sustained baseline QPS + bursts at 3x and 10x for 60s windows. Measure 429 rate, average queue time, and token truncation events.

Deliverables and timeline:
- By EOD Tue (2027-04-20): I’ll drop the test scripts (k6 scenarios) and a README.
- Wed (2027-04-21): run short smoke tests and share sample logs.
- Next week: run full runs with SafeHarbor workload sample.

I'll also add a short section in the matrix that calls out where Redwood's deterministic fallback policies differ from hyperscaler autoscale (single-sentence per row).

Marissa — can you capture the sample dashboard definitions (SLO windows and alert thresholds) we should push to their monitoring stack (Prom endpoint + recommended Grafana dashboards)?

-karthik

On a side note: attachment redwood-vs-hyperscaler-failover-matrix-20270418.xlsx looks good; I'll add a column for "expected operator action" so procurement can see what needs configuration vs enabled-by-default.
